Chapter Two: How Culture Shapes Gender Roles and Expectations
You know, culture is a force that runs deep—shaping not just how we see ourselves, but how we make sense of each other. Think about it: from the very start, kids learn what it “means” to be a boy or a girl. It isn’t always spelled out in words. Most of the time, it’s in the little things—those quiet signals from parents, friends, and the world around us.
Let’s picture a family get-together. The women are bustling around the kitchen, making sure everyone’s fed, while the men sit back, talking and laughing. No one ever says, “This is how it has to be”—but the message? It’s loud and clear. Certain jobs, certain roles, are just assumed to belong to certain people. So, imagine a young girl watching all this. She’s not handed a rulebook, but she gets it: her value is connected to serving others, maybe even staying quiet or out of the spotlight.
Then there’s school. The lessons don’t stop at home. If a girl shines in class, she might be told to dial it back, to not stand out too much. If she speaks her mind, she’s sometimes labeled “aggressive.” But if a boy does the same? He’s often praised for being confident. These double standards usually go unchallenged. It’s just “the way things are.”
As kids grow up, it gets even trickier. A teenage girl might be told not to wear certain clothes—not because it’s what she wants, but to avoid “sending the wrong message.” Suddenly, she’s responsible for how others act around her. Meanwhile, boys are told to be tough, to hide their feelings, to never seem weak. That kind of pressure? It’s real—and it shapes how they see themselves, and one another.
Most people don’t mean to push these roles—they’re just passing along what they learned, probably thinking it helps. But there’s a cost. Girls learn to make themselves smaller, to apologize for wanting more, to put everyone else first—even if it hurts them. Boys? They’re taught to bottle up their feelings, to measure their worth in strength and control. In the end, both sides lose something precious: the freedom to be fully themselves.
But sometimes, these roles get challenged. Maybe a girl goes after a career that’s “not for women.” Or a boy decides it’s okay to show vulnerability. The reaction? It might be surprise, maybe even a little pushback, or gentle nudges to get back “on track.” It takes guts to go against the grain—to imagine yourself living differently.
Here’s the hopeful part: culture isn’t set in stone. It shifts as people do. The first step? Just noticing the patterns, asking questions, and imagining new ways of being. When someone dares to say, “Why do we do it this way?”—that’s when change starts.
It’s not about blaming the past. It’s about opening up new choices, and building a future where everyone gets to be their whole, authentic self.
